title: CSEG3060 Group Assignment — Designing an Evidence-Based Computing Study (Units II & III)
instructions:
Work in groups of 2 to 5 students.

Choosing your topic — first come, first served:
  - The topics are listed at the top of this assignment. The first group to choose a topic gets it; it then shows as taken for everyone else.
  - Agree on a topic inside your group before choosing: any member can choose for the group, and the choice is final. Only your instructor can change it.
  - Once every listed topic has been taken, the remaining groups propose a topic of their own (a clear research question and a short description). Your instructor may ask you to revise it.
  - Writing opens once your group has a topic.

You will not run the study. You will design it rigorously and defend the design, using the methods of Unit II (argument, proof methods, reasoning, modelling, performance evaluation) and the literature and ethics practices of Unit III (systematic review, appraisal, synthesis, gap statement, integrity and ethics).

How you work:
  - Every member must write a real part of the text. The system records who wrote each paragraph, how much each member typed and when, and every member submits a private contribution declaration. Individual marks are adjusted by contribution.
  - Type your work here. Pasting from outside is blocked and logged. Put your PRISMA diagram, comparison spreadsheet, search logs and any figures in a shared Google Drive / OneDrive folder and add the link under Supplementary files, shared as 'anyone with the link can view'.
  - Cite every source in IEEE style, with a reference list at the end of the section that uses it. At least 8 peer-reviewed papers from the last five years must be reviewed in Section 3.
  - AI-generated content is limited to 20% of the work (UPES policy). Declare any AI tool you used, and for what, in Section 6. Undeclared use is treated as an integrity violation.
  - Similarity above 10% (excluding references and quoted material) is reported under the UGC 2018 regulations.

topics.title: LLM code assistants vs novice programmers
topics.description: Do LLM-based code assistants produce functionally correct code for data-structure tasks more often than novice programmers?

topics.title: Federated learning for medical imaging
topics.description: Can federated learning match centralised training accuracy for medical-image classification while keeping patient data on-site?

topics.title: Generalisation of ML intrusion detection
topics.description: How well do ML intrusion-detection systems trained on CIC-IDS2017 generalise to a different network dataset?

topics.title: Edge caching for campus video streaming
topics.description: Does edge caching reduce end-to-end latency for campus video streaming, and at what cache size does the benefit stop?

topics.title: Quantised neural networks on mobile devices
topics.description: Do quantised (8-bit) neural networks give acceptable accuracy on mobile devices while cutting energy use?

topics.title: Blockchain consensus for supply-chain ledgers
topics.description: Which blockchain consensus mechanism gives the best throughput-to-energy ratio for permissioned supply-chain ledgers?

topics.title: Deepfake detection under compression
topics.description: Are deepfake-detection models robust to the video compression used by social-media platforms?

topics.title: Cold-start fairness in recommender systems
topics.description: Do popularity-based recommender systems treat new (cold-start) items and users unfairly compared with content-based ones?

questions.question:
Section 1 — Research question and the claim you will defend.

State your group's topic as a precise research question and frame it with PICO (or PCC if your question is exploratory). Explain why the question matters and which of the three paradigms of computing (theory, abstraction, design) it belongs to. Finish with the single central claim your study would try to establish, written as a testable hypothesis.
questions.guidance: About 300–450 words. The claim must be specific enough that evidence could prove it wrong.
questions.starter:
## Research question
## PICO / PCC framing
## Why it matters
## Paradigm of computing
## Central claim (hypothesis)
questions.modelAnswer: Question stated precisely and matches the group's chosen topic (0.5). PICO/PCC elements all present and correctly identified — P, I, C, O or P, C, C (1). Significance argued with at least one cited source (1). Paradigm correctly identified with a reason (0.5). Hypothesis is testable and falsifiable, names the variables and the direction of effect (1). Deduct for a vague claim such as 'X is better'.

questions.question:
Section 2 — Systematic literature search.

Write the review protocol for your question: the databases searched (e.g. IEEE Xplore, ACM DL, Scopus, arXiv), the exact search strings with Boolean operators, the inclusion and exclusion criteria, and the date range. Report the screening as a PRISMA flow: numbers identified, duplicates removed, screened, excluded (with reasons) and included. Put the PRISMA diagram itself in your shared drive and link it.
questions.guidance: About 300–500 words plus a table of the PRISMA counts. Someone else must be able to repeat your search from what you write.
questions.starter:
## Review type and why we chose it
## Databases and date range
## Search strings
## Inclusion and exclusion criteria
## PRISMA flow (counts)
questions.modelAnswer: Review type (systematic / scoping) named and justified against the alternatives (1). At least three databases and a date range (0.5). Search strings are real, reproducible and use Boolean operators and synonyms (1). Inclusion/exclusion criteria are explicit and justified (1). PRISMA counts are internally consistent (identified − duplicates − exclusions = included) and reasons for exclusion are given (1). PRISMA diagram linked (0.5).

questions.question:
Section 3 — Critical appraisal, synthesis and the research gap.

Appraise at least eight of the included papers through the three lenses (methodological, conceptual, contribution) and summarise them in a comparison table (paper, method, dataset/workload, metric, key result, main limitation). Then synthesise: group the papers by approach and say where they agree, where they conflict and why. End with a precise gap statement in the form taught in class.
questions.guidance: About 700–1100 words plus the table. Synthesis, not a paper-by-paper summary. Cite in IEEE style.
questions.starter:
## Comparison table
## Appraisal highlights
## Synthesis by approach
## Where the literature agrees and conflicts
## Research gap statement
## References
questions.modelAnswer: ≥ 8 relevant peer-reviewed papers from the last five years (1). Comparison table complete and accurate for all columns (1.5). Appraisal uses all three lenses and names concrete weaknesses, not only strengths (1.5). Synthesis is organised by theme/approach and explains conflicts (e.g. different datasets, baselines or metrics) (2). Gap statement follows the taught grammar, is specific, and follows from the synthesis rather than being asserted (1). Deduct heavily for an annotated bibliography with no synthesis.

questions.question:
Section 4 — The argument and the proof method.

Lay out your central claim as a Toulmin argument (claim, evidence you would collect, warrant, backing, qualifier, rebuttal). Choose the proof method your study needs — demonstration, empirical or mathematical — and justify why the other two are not sufficient on their own. Identify where your study reasons deductively, inductively and abductively, and describe one turn of the hypothetico-deductive cycle for it. Name two logical fallacies your argument must avoid and how you will avoid them.
questions.guidance: About 500–800 words. Use your own topic throughout — generic definitions earn little.
questions.starter:
## Toulmin model of our claim
## Proof method and why
## Deduction, induction and abduction in our study
## One cycle of the hypothetico-deductive method
## Fallacies we must avoid
questions.modelAnswer: All six Toulmin elements present and applied to the group's own claim; the warrant genuinely links evidence to claim (1.5). Proof method chosen correctly for the question, with reasons why the other two are insufficient (1). Deductive, inductive and abductive steps correctly identified in the study (1). Hypothetico-deductive cycle traced with a concrete prediction (0.5). Two relevant fallacies (e.g. hasty generalisation, cherry-picking, false cause) with a concrete safeguard for each (1).

questions.question:
Section 5 — Model and performance-evaluation plan.

Build a simple mathematical model of the system or phenomenon you study (for example a queueing model, Little's Law, Amdahl's Law, a cost or accuracy model) and state its assumptions and what it predicts. Then design the performance evaluation that would test that prediction: metrics, workload characterisation, baseline(s), factors and levels, number of repetitions, how you will report variability (e.g. confidence intervals), and the threats to validity (internal, external, construct, conclusion) with a mitigation for each.
questions.guidance: About 500–800 words. Include at least one equation (use the √x equation tool) and one table of factors and levels.
questions.starter:
## Model and assumptions
## What the model predicts
## Metrics and workload
## Baselines, factors and levels
## Repetitions and statistical reporting
## Threats to validity and mitigations
questions.modelAnswer: Model appropriate to the question, equation stated, assumptions explicit, and a quantitative prediction derived (1.5). Metrics measure the claim and workload is characterised (1). A fair, recent baseline; factors/levels table sensible (1). Repetitions and variability reporting (CIs or equivalent) specified (0.5). All four threat categories addressed with credible mitigations (1). Deduct for common mistakes listed in the notes (no baseline, single run, unrepresentative workload).

questions.question:
Section 6 — Ethics, integrity and our use of sources.

Apply the three Belmont principles (respect for persons, beneficence, justice) to your study. Decide whether it would need Institutional Ethics Committee review and at what level, and why. Address data protection (DPDP Act 2023), licences and intellectual property of datasets, code and models you would use, and the risks specific to your topic. Then describe your group's integrity workflow: how you paraphrased and cited (IEEE), which reference manager you used, and the similarity-check result if you ran one. End with an honest declaration of any AI tools used, what for, and roughly how much of the work they shaped.
questions.guidance: About 400–650 words. Specific to your study, not a general essay on ethics.
questions.starter:
## Belmont principles applied to our study
## Does it need IEC review?
## Data protection and intellectual property
## Risks specific to our topic
## Our integrity workflow
## Declaration of AI use
questions.modelAnswer: Each Belmont principle applied concretely to this study (1). IEC decision correct with the review level and reasoning (0.5). DPDP, dataset/code/model licences and IP addressed specifically (1). Topic-specific risks identified (e.g. bias, dual use, privacy) (0.5). Integrity workflow is concrete — citation style, reference manager, similarity check (0.5). AI-use declaration present and plausible (0.5).
